newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. military says closely watching Spratlys.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military says closely watching Spratlys.

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in the Pacific said on Thursday rival claims over the resources of the South China Sea could cause friction and the United States was keenly watching the situation.
Admiral Joseph Prueher said, however, he was "very hopeful" an understanding among claimants to peacefully settle their differences would lead to a resolution of their disputes.

"I think the energy interest of all the countries for gas and oil explorations...is something that has the possibility of friction, but right now it looks like it's been worked in a peaceful way, in a way that will yield stability," Prueher told a news conference.
"We watch it very carefully," he added.
Diplomats regard the South China Sea, believed to be rich in oil and gas, as a potential flashpoint because of rival claims over the area by at least six nations.

China and Vietnam are squabbling over the Paracel Islands. They are also locked in a separate dispute with Malaysia, Taiwan, the Philippines and Brunei over ownership of all or part of the adjacent Spratly Islands.
Prueher said the South China Sea was a vital commercial sea lane for about 400 ships that pass through it every day.

"The U.S. view is that the nations involved need to work out the sovereignty issues," he said. "The United States is keenly watching and very interested in the issues of freedom of navigation and freedom of the sea and are committed to working on those issues."

He said he was "very optimistic" about the overall security situation in the Asia-Pacific region and that arms buying by countries did not mean an arms race was going on. These were part of their efforts to modernise their armies for "legitimate defence needs," he added.
"There are a lot of challenges ahead and I think that if all of the nations together work on them constructively and well, we can continue to have stability in the Asia-Pacific region."
"There is also opportunity, as always, to sour it up and I hope we don't do that."
